title: Advanced Microbial Genetics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Advanced Microbial Genetics curriculum: gene regulation (operon models, attenuation), mutation and DNA repair mechanisms, horizontal gene transfer (transformation, conjugation, transduction), plasmids and transposons, bacteriophage genetics, and recombinant DNA/gene cloning technology -- building on introductory genetics with molecular mechanistic depth.

questions.question: In the lac operon model of gene regulation in E. coli, in the absence of lactose (and allolactose), the lac repressor protein:
options: Is inactive and cannot bind DNA
Binds the operator sequence, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA)
Binds directly to the promoter and enhances transcription
Degrades the lac mRNA after it is made
questions.correct_answer: Binds the operator sequence, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA)
questions.explanation: In the absence of an inducer, the active lac repressor binds tightly to the operator, sterically blocking RNA polymerase from proceeding into the structural genes, keeping the operon off (negative control).

questions.question: Allolactose, the natural inducer of the lac operon, activates the operon by:
options: Binding the lac repressor and causing a conformational change that reduces its affinity for the operator, releasing it from the DNA
Binding directly to RNA polymerase
Destroying the operator sequence permanently
Binding CAP (catabolite activator protein) to inactivate it
questions.correct_answer: Binding the lac repressor and causing a conformational change that reduces its affinity for the operator, releasing it from the DNA
questions.explanation: Allolactose binds an allosteric site on the lac repressor, changing its shape so it can no longer bind the operator with high affinity; the repressor dissociates from the DNA, allowing transcription to proceed.

questions.question: Catabolite repression of the lac operon (glucose effect) works through the cAMP-CAP (catabolite activator protein) system: when glucose is abundant, intracellular cAMP levels are:
options: High, strongly activating CAP-dependent transcription
Low, so CAP cannot bind cAMP and activate transcription, keeping catabolic operons for alternative sugars like lactose only weakly transcribed even if the inducer is present
Unaffected by glucose availability
Irrelevant, since CAP does not require cAMP to function
questions.correct_answer: Low, so CAP cannot bind cAMP and activate transcription, keeping catabolic operons for alternative sugars like lactose only weakly transcribed even if the inducer is present
questions.explanation: High glucose lowers cAMP levels; with little cAMP available, CAP cannot form the active cAMP-CAP complex needed to bind its DNA site and enhance RNA polymerase binding at the lac promoter, so lac operon expression stays low even when lactose/inducer is present, ensuring glucose is used preferentially.

questions.question: The trp operon, which encodes enzymes for tryptophan biosynthesis, is primarily regulated by:
options: Positive control only, with no repressor
A repressor that becomes active (able to bind the operator) only when bound to tryptophan itself (a corepressor), shutting off the operon when tryptophan is abundant
A repressor that is inactivated by tryptophan binding
Catabolite repression exclusively
questions.correct_answer: A repressor that becomes active (able to bind the operator) only when bound to tryptophan itself (a corepressor), shutting off the operon when tryptophan is abundant
questions.explanation: The trp repressor is inactive alone; when tryptophan (the pathway's end product) is plentiful, it binds the repressor as a corepressor, activating it to bind the operator and repress further trp operon transcription -- classic end-product-mediated negative feedback control.

questions.question: Attenuation, an additional fine-tuning mechanism controlling the trp operon beyond repression, works at the level of:
options: DNA replication

Premature termination of transcription in the leader region, modulated by the ribosome's translation rate over a leader peptide sequence rich in tryptophan codons, coupling transcription to translation
Post-translational protein degradation
mRNA capping in the nucleus
questions.correct_answer: Premature termination of transcription in the leader region, modulated by the ribosome's translation rate over a leader peptide sequence rich in tryptophan codons, coupling transcription to translation
questions.explanation: Attenuation exploits coupled transcription-translation in bacteria: when tryptophan (and charged tRNA-Trp) is abundant, the ribosome translates the leader peptide's Trp codons quickly, favouring formation of a terminator hairpin that halts transcription; when tryptophan is scarce, ribosome stalling favours an antiterminator structure, allowing transcription to continue.

questions.question: A point mutation that changes a codon so that it now specifies a different amino acid is classified as a:
options: Silent mutation
Missense mutation
Nonsense mutation
Frameshift mutation
questions.correct_answer: Missense mutation
questions.explanation: A missense mutation is a base substitution that alters a codon such that a different amino acid is incorporated into the protein, potentially affecting protein structure/function, in contrast to a silent mutation (no amino acid change) or nonsense mutation (premature stop codon).

questions.question: A nonsense mutation results in:
options: No change in the encoded protein
A premature stop codon, causing truncation of the protein at that point
Insertion of an extra amino acid
A shift in the reading frame of the entire downstream sequence
questions.correct_answer: A premature stop codon, causing truncation of the protein at that point
questions.explanation: Nonsense mutations convert a sense codon into one of the three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), causing translation to terminate prematurely and producing a truncated, usually non-functional, protein.

questions.question: Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three within a coding sequence causes a:
options: Silent mutation with no phenotypic effect
Frameshift mutation, altering the reading frame for all downstream codons and usually producing a severely altered, non-functional protein
Missense mutation affecting only a single codon
Reversion to wild type
questions.correct_answer: Frameshift mutation, altering the reading frame for all downstream codons and usually producing a severely altered, non-functional protein
questions.explanation: Because codons are read as non-overlapping triplets, insertion or deletion of a number of bases not divisible by three shifts the reading frame from that point onward, typically scrambling the amino acid sequence and often introducing a premature stop codon.

questions.question: Ultraviolet (UV) light is mutagenic mainly because it induces formation of:
options: Double-strand breaks exclusively
Pyrimidine (commonly thymine) dimers, covalent linkages between adjacent pyrimidine bases on the same DNA strand that distort the helix and block replication/transcription unless repaired
Alkylated purine bases
Deletion of entire genes
questions.correct_answer: Pyrimidine (commonly thymine) dimers, covalent linkages between adjacent pyrimidine bases on the same DNA strand that distort the helix and block replication/transcription unless repaired
questions.explanation: UV radiation is absorbed by DNA and promotes covalent bonding between adjacent pyrimidine bases, forming dimers (most commonly thymine dimers) that distort the double helix and stall replication or transcription unless removed by repair mechanisms.

questions.question: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) corrects bulky DNA lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers by:
options: Directly reversing the dimer back to two separate bases using a single enzyme, without removing any DNA
Excising a short single-stranded segment of DNA containing the lesion and resynthesising it using the undamaged complementary strand as a template
Deleting the entire chromosome
Converting the damaged base into a different, harmless base chemically
questions.correct_answer: Excising a short single-stranded segment of DNA containing the lesion and resynthesising it using the undamaged complementary strand as a template
questions.explanation: NER uses a multi-enzyme complex to recognise a helix-distorting lesion, cut the damaged strand on both sides of it, remove the segment, and use DNA polymerase and ligase to fill and seal the gap using the intact complementary strand as template.

questions.question: Photoreactivation (light repair) of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers is carried out by the enzyme:
options: DNA polymerase I only
Photolyase, which uses energy absorbed from visible light to directly reverse (split) the dimer back into two normal, separate bases
Ligase, independent of any light
Reverse transcriptase
questions.correct_answer: Photolyase, which uses energy absorbed from visible light to directly reverse (split) the dimer back into two normal, separate bases
questions.explanation: Photolyase binds a pyrimidine dimer and, using energy captured from visible/blue light, directly breaks the covalent bonds joining the two pyrimidines, restoring the original bases without excising any DNA -- a light-dependent repair mechanism distinct from excision repair.

questions.question: The SOS response in bacteria, triggered by extensive DNA damage, involves:
options: Permanent shutdown of all DNA repair genes
Induction of a coordinated set of DNA repair and damage-tolerance genes, controlled by cleavage of the LexA repressor mediated by activated RecA, sometimes including error-prone translesion synthesis
Immediate cell death with no attempt at repair
Complete replication arrest with no gene expression changes
questions.correct_answer: Induction of a coordinated set of DNA repair and damage-tolerance genes, controlled by cleavage of the LexA repressor mediated by activated RecA, sometimes including error-prone translesion synthesis
questions.explanation: Extensive DNA damage activates RecA, which promotes autocleavage of the LexA repressor; this derepresses a regulon of SOS genes including additional repair enzymes and, in extreme cases, error-prone DNA polymerases that allow replication past unrepaired lesions at the cost of increased mutation rate.

questions.question: Bacterial transformation refers to the process by which a bacterium:
options: Acquires new genetic material by direct cell-to-cell contact through a pilus
Takes up free (naked) DNA from its surrounding environment and incorporates it into its genome or maintains it as a plasmid
Receives DNA injected by a bacteriophage
Randomly mutates its own DNA without any external source
questions.correct_answer: Takes up free (naked) DNA from its surrounding environment and incorporates it into its genome or maintains it as a plasmid
questions.explanation: Transformation is the uptake of extracellular, cell-free DNA (released, for example, from lysed cells) by a competent recipient bacterium, which may then recombine the DNA into its chromosome or maintain it episomally.

questions.question: Natural genetic competence, the physiological state allowing a bacterium to take up extracellular DNA, is a well-studied trait of organisms such as:
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Bacillus subtilis
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Human erythrocytes
Bacteriophage lambda
questions.correct_answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Bacillus subtilis
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the organism in which transformation was first discovered by Griffith and later molecularly explained by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty) and Bacillus subtilis are classic model organisms exhibiting natural genetic competence.

questions.question: Bacterial conjugation, the transfer of DNA from a donor to a recipient cell via direct cell-to-cell contact, requires the donor to possess:
options: A bacteriophage genome integrated into its chromosome
A conjugative (fertility) plasmid, such as the F plasmid, that encodes the machinery (including the sex pilus) needed to form a mating bridge with the recipient
No special genetic elements at all
A capsule
questions.correct_answer: A conjugative (fertility) plasmid, such as the F plasmid, that encodes the machinery (including the sex pilus) needed to form a mating bridge with the recipient
questions.explanation: Conjugation requires the donor cell to carry a conjugative plasmid (the classic example being the F plasmid), whose tra genes encode the sex pilus and transfer apparatus that establish contact with, and transfer DNA into, the recipient cell.

questions.question: An Hfr (high-frequency recombination) strain of E. coli arises when:
options: The F plasmid is lost entirely from the cell
The F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome, so that conjugation can transfer chromosomal genes at high frequency starting from the integration site
A bacteriophage infects the cell and lysogenises it
The cell undergoes binary fission twice in succession
questions.correct_answer: The F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome, so that conjugation can transfer chromosomal genes at high frequency starting from the integration site
questions.explanation: When the F plasmid recombines into the host chromosome (via homologous IS sequences), the resulting Hfr strain, during conjugation, transfers chromosomal DNA (rather than just plasmid DNA) into the recipient starting from the integration point, enabling chromosomal gene mapping by timed mating experiments.

questions.question: Generalized transduction is a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer in which:
options: A bacteriophage mistakenly packages a random fragment of host bacterial DNA instead of (or along with) its own genome during the lytic cycle, and transfers this to a new host upon infection
DNA passes directly between two bacteria through a conjugation pilus
Free DNA is taken up from the environment
Only phage genes, never host genes, are transferred
questions.correct_answer: A bacteriophage mistakenly packages a random fragment of host bacterial DNA instead of (or along with) its own genome during the lytic cycle, and transfers this to a new host upon infection
questions.explanation: During generalized transduction, errors in the phage packaging machinery cause random host chromosomal DNA fragments to be encapsulated into phage particles instead of phage DNA; when such a particle infects a new host, it can inject the donor's bacterial DNA, allowing recombination into the recipient's genome.

questions.question: Specialized transduction, in contrast to generalized transduction, transfers only specific host genes because it occurs when:
options: A lysogenic (temperate) phage's prophage excises imprecisely from a specific chromosomal location, carrying adjacent host genes along with phage DNA into new virions
Any random phage infects a cell lytically
Conjugation occurs between an Hfr donor and F- recipient
A plasmid is lost during cell division
questions.correct_answer: A lysogenic (temperate) phage's prophage excises imprecisely from a specific chromosomal location, carrying adjacent host genes along with phage DNA into new virions
questions.explanation: Specialized transduction depends on a temperate phage's prophage, integrated at a fixed chromosomal site; occasional imprecise excision picks up host genes flanking that specific integration site, so only those particular genes (not random ones) are transferred, unlike generalized transduction.

questions.question: Plasmids are defined as:
options: Essential chromosomal genes required for basic cell survival

Extrachromosomal, typically circular, double-stranded DNA molecules capable of autonomous (independent) replication, often carrying non-essential but potentially advantageous genes such as antibiotic resistance
Fragments of RNA found only in viruses
Structural proteins of the bacterial cell wall
questions.correct_answer: Extrachromosomal, typically circular, double-stranded DNA molecules capable of autonomous (independent) replication, often carrying non-essential but potentially advantageous genes such as antibiotic resistance
questions.explanation: Plasmids are self-replicating extrachromosomal DNA elements, usually circular, that are not essential for basic cell viability but often confer selective advantages, such as antibiotic resistance (R plasmids) or virulence factors.

questions.question: Transposons ('jumping genes') differ from plasmids in that transposons:
options: Are always circular and replicate independently of the chromosome

Are DNA segments that can move from one location to another within or between DNA molecules (chromosome/plasmid) via a cut-and-paste or copy-and-paste mechanism, without independent replication of their own
Cannot carry any genes
Only exist in eukaryotic cells
questions.correct_answer: Are DNA segments that can move from one location to another within or between DNA molecules (chromosome/plasmid) via a cut-and-paste or copy-and-paste mechanism, without independent replication of their own
questions.explanation: Transposons are mobile genetic elements that relocate within a genome (or between chromosome and plasmid) using transposase-mediated mechanisms, but unlike plasmids they do not replicate autonomously as independent replicons; they are replicated as part of whatever DNA molecule currently carries them.

questions.question: Insertion sequences (IS elements), the simplest type of bacterial transposable element, typically contain:
options: Only genes for antibiotic resistance
A gene encoding transposase flanked by inverted repeat sequences, with no additional accessory genes
A complete bacteriophage genome
An entire set of ribosomal RNA genes
questions.correct_answer: A gene encoding transposase flanked by inverted repeat sequences, with no additional accessory genes
questions.explanation: IS elements are the simplest transposons, consisting essentially of a transposase gene flanked by short inverted repeats that are recognised by the transposase; unlike composite transposons, they do not carry additional accessory genes such as antibiotic resistance markers.

questions.question: R plasmids (resistance plasmids), of major clinical and public health concern, typically carry genes that:
options: Confer resistance to one or more antibiotics and can be transferred between bacteria, including different species, via conjugation
Are essential for basic bacterial metabolism and cannot be lost
Encode only bacteriophage receptor proteins
Cannot be transferred between cells under any circumstances
questions.correct_answer: Confer resistance to one or more antibiotics and can be transferred between bacteria, including different species, via conjugation
questions.explanation: R plasmids carry one or more antibiotic resistance genes and, if conjugative, can spread these resistance traits horizontally between bacterial cells and even across species boundaries, a major driver of the spread of antimicrobial resistance.

questions.question: A lytic bacteriophage, upon infecting a susceptible bacterial host, characteristically:
options: Integrates its genome into the host chromosome and remains dormant indefinitely
Replicates immediately, directs the host machinery to produce new phage particles, and then lyses the host cell to release progeny virions
Never produces new phage particles
Converts the host into a plant cell
questions.correct_answer: Replicates immediately, directs the host machinery to produce new phage particles, and then lyses the host cell to release progeny virions
questions.explanation: In the lytic cycle, the phage hijacks host replication and translation machinery to produce many copies of itself, then triggers cell lysis (often via phage-encoded lysozyme-like enzymes) to release the new virions to infect further host cells.

questions.question: A temperate bacteriophage such as lambda phage differs from a strictly lytic phage in that it can also:
options: Only infect eukaryotic cells
Establish lysogeny, integrating its genome into the host chromosome as a prophage that is replicated passively along with the host DNA, until induced to enter the lytic cycle
Never replicate its DNA at all
Only exist as free RNA in the cytoplasm
questions.correct_answer: Establish lysogeny, integrating its genome into the host chromosome as a prophage that is replicated passively along with the host DNA, until induced to enter the lytic cycle
questions.explanation: Temperate phages can choose between the lytic cycle and lysogeny; in lysogeny, the phage genome integrates as a prophage and is stably replicated with the host chromosome across generations, until an inducing signal (e.g. DNA damage/SOS response) triggers excision and entry into the lytic cycle.

questions.question: Lysogenic conversion refers to the phenomenon in which:
options: A prophage confers a new phenotype on its lysogenic host, such as toxin production, by genes it carries (e.g. diphtheria toxin encoded by a prophage in Corynebacterium diphtheriae)
A phage loses its ability to lyse host cells permanently
Bacteria become resistant to all phages after lysogeny
A plasmid is converted into a phage
questions.correct_answer: A prophage confers a new phenotype on its lysogenic host, such as toxin production, by genes it carries (e.g. diphtheria toxin encoded by a prophage in Corynebacterium diphtheriae)
questions.explanation: Lysogenic conversion occurs when a prophage carries and expresses genes that change the host's phenotype; a classic example is the tox gene carried by a lysogenic corynebacteriophage, which enables Corynebacterium diphtheriae to produce diphtheria toxin.

questions.question: Restriction endonucleases, essential tools in recombinant DNA technology, function by:
options: Joining DNA fragments together permanently
Recognising specific short DNA sequences and cleaving the DNA at or near that sequence, often generating fragments with complementary 'sticky ends'
Synthesising new DNA strands from a template
Amplifying DNA exponentially using thermal cycling
questions.correct_answer: Recognising specific short DNA sequences and cleaving the DNA at or near that sequence, often generating fragments with complementary 'sticky ends'
questions.explanation: Restriction endonucleases recognise specific palindromic DNA sequences and cut the DNA backbone at defined positions; many produce staggered cuts leaving short single-stranded 'sticky ends' that can base-pair with complementary ends generated by the same enzyme, facilitating recombinant DNA construction.

questions.question: In molecular cloning, DNA ligase is used to:
options: Cut DNA at specific recognition sites
Covalently join (seal) the phosphodiester backbone between a DNA insert and a vector, forming a stable recombinant DNA molecule
Amplify DNA fragments exponentially
Separate DNA fragments by size on a gel
questions.correct_answer: Covalently join (seal) the phosphodiester backbone between a DNA insert and a vector, forming a stable recombinant DNA molecule
questions.explanation: DNA ligase catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, sealing nicks where a DNA insert (e.g. a gene of interest) has been annealed to a cut vector, producing an intact, covalently closed recombinant DNA molecule.

questions.question: A plasmid cloning vector used in recombinant DNA work should ideally possess:
options: No selectable marker genes at all
An origin of replication, one or more selectable marker genes (e.g. antibiotic resistance), and unique restriction sites (often within a multiple cloning site) for inserting foreign DNA
The ability to integrate randomly into any host chromosome, destroying host genes
A requirement for host cell death to replicate
questions.correct_answer: An origin of replication, one or more selectable marker genes (e.g. antibiotic resistance), and unique restriction sites (often within a multiple cloning site) for inserting foreign DNA
questions.explanation: A good plasmid cloning vector needs an origin of replication for autonomous propagation in the host, a selectable marker to identify cells that have taken up the plasmid, and convenient unique restriction sites to allow insertion of foreign DNA fragments.

questions.question: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) exponentially amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro using repeated cycles of:
options: Restriction digestion, ligation, and transformation
Denaturation (heating to separate DNA strands), primer annealing (cooling to allow specific primers to bind), and extension (heat-stable DNA polymerase synthesising new complementary strands)
Gel electrophoresis followed by Southern blotting
Conjugation between bacterial donor and recipient cells
questions.correct_answer: Denaturation (heating to separate DNA strands), primer annealing (cooling to allow specific primers to bind), and extension (heat-stable DNA polymerase synthesising new complementary strands)
questions.explanation: PCR uses repeated thermal cycles of denaturation, primer annealing, and extension by a thermostable DNA polymerase (commonly Taq polymerase), doubling the target DNA sequence with each cycle to achieve exponential amplification of a specific region.

questions.question: Taq DNA polymerase, widely used in PCR, is prized for its:
options: Inability to withstand heat, requiring fresh enzyme every cycle
Thermostability, allowing it to survive repeated cycles of high-temperature DNA denaturation (around 94-98°C) without being destroyed
Ability to repair mutations perfectly with zero error rate
Requirement for a eukaryotic host cell to function
questions.correct_answer: Thermostability, allowing it to survive repeated cycles of high-temperature DNA denaturation (around 94-98°C) without being destroyed
questions.explanation: Taq polymerase, originally isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, remains active despite the repeated high-temperature denaturation steps of PCR, eliminating the need to add fresh enzyme after each cycle, unlike heat-labile polymerases.

questions.question: The CRISPR-Cas9 system, originally a bacterial/archaeal adaptive immune mechanism against bacteriophages, has been adapted as a genome-editing tool because Cas9:
options: Is a restriction enzyme that only cuts plasmid DNA
Can be guided by a programmable RNA sequence (guide RNA) to introduce a precise double-strand break at a specific, complementary DNA target sequence
Only functions to ligate DNA fragments together
Cannot be reprogrammed to target new sequences
questions.correct_answer: Can be guided by a programmable RNA sequence (guide RNA) to introduce a precise double-strand break at a specific, complementary DNA target sequence
questions.explanation: Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease: a synthetic guide RNA directs it to bind a complementary DNA sequence (adjacent to a PAM site) and introduce a targeted double-strand break, which can then be exploited for gene disruption or precise editing via cellular repair pathways.

questions.question: In bacteria, CRISPR loci naturally function as an adaptive immune system by:
options: Permanently silencing all foreign DNA regardless of sequence

Storing short sequences ('spacers') derived from previously encountered phage or plasmid DNA, which are later transcribed and used by Cas proteins to recognise and cleave matching invading DNA upon reinfection
Producing antibodies against phage proteins
Preventing conjugation entirely
questions.correct_answer: Storing short sequences ('spacers') derived from previously encountered phage or plasmid DNA, which are later transcribed and used by Cas proteins to recognise and cleave matching invading DNA upon reinfection
questions.explanation: CRISPR arrays incorporate short spacer sequences captured from past invading genetic elements; these are transcribed into guide RNAs that direct Cas nucleases to recognise and destroy matching sequences in subsequently invading phage or plasmid DNA, providing sequence-specific, heritable immunity.

questions.question: Riboswitches, found in the untranslated regions of some bacterial mRNAs, regulate gene expression by:
options: Requiring a separate regulatory protein to bind DNA
Directly binding a small metabolite ligand, causing a conformational change in the mRNA that affects transcription termination or translation initiation without any protein intermediate
Encoding a transposase enzyme
Functioning only in eukaryotic cells
questions.correct_answer: Directly binding a small metabolite ligand, causing a conformational change in the mRNA that affects transcription termination or translation initiation without any protein intermediate
questions.explanation: Riboswitches are RNA elements that directly sense small metabolites (e.g. amino acids, vitamins, nucleotides); ligand binding changes the mRNA's secondary structure, altering whether transcription is terminated prematurely or the ribosome-binding site is accessible, regulating gene expression without needing a protein sensor.
